source.title: SIEVE: Selective attention-value Suppression for Vision-Language Models Unlearning
source.authors: Si-Qi Goh; Cap Dang Xuan Kiet; Tat-Jen Cham; Kwok-Yan Lam

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Figure 9 is referenced, but its visual contents are not available in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates a different unlearning intervention and includes a manual attention-map attack relevant to internal-access recovery, rather than reproducing the attacks in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports ordinary forget-set and retain-set performance for SIEVE, and describes implementing a manual attention-map attack. It does not test recovery by fine-tuning, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompting alone. Its figure-only attack result cannot be assessed from the supplied text. Baseline-method comparisons are not separately cataloged except where needed as reference values.
record.test_reason: A new VLM unlearning method (SIEVE) on MLLMU-Bench with selective, attribute-level forget/retain splits. Its forget/retain scores bear on version A in a new multimodal setting. Its Test split (GPT-4o-paraphrased questions plus Arc2Face-altered images) bears on whether rephrasing recovers forgotten facts (E). The attention-map attack sits near C, but its result appears only in a figure.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that attention-value suppression with reference-based preservation gives state-of-the-art selective forgetting with competitive retained utility across VLMs and modalities. They list stronger evaluation of residual-information recovery as future work, and say their toy analysis does not establish robustness to attention-map attacks.
record.recipe_differences: SIEVE is a new selective VLM unlearning method: it suppresses attention-value representations for forget examples, matches retain representations to a frozen reference, and adds sequence-level forget/retain objectives. It is not a replication of the original methods in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Results are reported separately across Visual-QA and Textual-QA, model backbones and sizes, and evaluation splits; the paper also reports different outcomes across classification, generation, and cloze metrics.

fits_no_version.finding: A key-suppression variant forgets as well as value suppression (21.13 vs 20.06) but loses more retain utility, e.g. retain cloze 5.51 vs 27.95.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The choice of attention component suppressed (key vs value) shifts the forgetting–utility trade-off.

record.problems: No chance-level reference is reported for the forget accuracy results. The manual attention-map attack is only available as a figure reference in the supplied text, so its outcome cannot be assessed. The benchmark's training forget set consists of fictitious profiles; results are not reported with uncertainty for the claim-related performance metrics.
record.rows_left_out: Generation and cloze scores, other evaluation splits, and comparator unlearning-method scores are omitted; the extracted rows focus on classification accuracy for the claim's accuracy/utility wording and the separate manual attention-map attack. Table 1 and Table 8 contain the omitted metrics and splits.

untested.parts: No chance-level reference. Only paraphrase/image-shift evaluation is used as an attack; no adversarial attacks on the unlearned model.
No activation-direction ablation or probing for residual knowledge. The attention-map attack result is figure-only.
No jailbreaks, other languages or in-context information. Only the paraphrased and image-altered Test split is evaluated.
No resistance claims against fine-tuning, ablation, quantization or prompting attacks.

missing.what: Test-split (paraphrased plus altered-image) forget-attribute classification, generation and cloze for SIEVE vs vanilla in all model–modality settings; bears on rephrasing-based recovery.
missing.locator: Table 1 Test columns; Table 8 Test columns; Appendix B.3

missing.what: Forget-set generation ROUGE stays fairly high after SIEVE (e.g. 0.430 vs 0.552 on LLaVA-7B Visual-QA), a weaker reduction than classification shows.
Real (celebrity) set utility, the closest proxy for general ability, e.g. 43.90 vs 46.21.

record.verdict_notes: This is primarily a new-method paper. Chance level for the multiple-choice task is not stated in the text; if MLLMU-Bench uses 4 options, about 25% applies, which would make the LLaVA-7B forget scores roughly chance. The E verdicts rest on a benchmark generalization split that combines paraphrasing with image edits, not a pure prompting attack.

versions.untested_parts: No chance-level reference is given, and post-unlearning recovery attacks are not evaluated as part of these ordinary forget/retain scores.
No recovery fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples is tested.

The study tests manual attention-map manipulation, not ablation of an activation direction. It does not establish that the targeted information is deleted from weights or that no other recovery route exists.
No low-bit quantization experiment is reported.
No recovery by rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information is tested.
The study does not test resistance to the listed fine-tuning, activation-ablation, quantization, or prompting attacks.

relation.reason: Reports forget/retain accuracy and a paraphrase-plus-image shifted Test split that bear on versions A and E.

tranche.reason: SIEVE is a new method in a new multimodal setting (VLMs on MLLMU-Bench), with forget, retain and shifted-test results bearing on the claim. T2 would also be defensible.

source_check.notes: Table 1 is flattened. Cells were placed by row order and confirmed against the text (25.50, 0.349, 28.03, 0.33, 3.25). The Test split is a benchmark generalization split (GPT-4o paraphrases plus Arc2Face images of the Forget set), not an attack applied after unlearning. The paper doesn't say whether Test items cover only forget attributes: Test has 1024 Visual and 490 Textual items, against 764 and 488 for Forget. The E reading depends on the metric: Test cloze falls 21.33 to 9.67 on LLaVA-7B Visual and only 21.47 to 19.27 on LLaVA-7B Textual. No chance level is given.

statements.correction: SIEVE, MLLMU-Bench, selective attribute-level forgetting, preprint, no code: LLaVA-1.5-7B Visual-QA forget classification 69.67 to 20.06, retain 43.75 to 39.20 (Table 1); no chance level stated. Same cell, Test split (GPT-4o paraphrases, Arc2Face images): classification 50.16 to 44.43. Weaker forgetting on Qwen2-VL-7B Textual-QA (53.63 to 38.98) and LLaVA-1.5-13B (Visual 62.82 to 31.53, Textual 68.73 to 35.99; Table 8).
statements.problem: Cites R1 as multimodal support for A but gives no figure for this study (all numbers are CUSE, SafeEraser, HFRU, PPE-Bench). In that same cell, the paraphrase+Arc2Face Test split keeps most classification accuracy, so this study does not show that simple shifts fail to recover.
